questions.question: What is a sequence $(a_n)_{n\geq m}$?
options: An unordered collection of elements $a_n$ with $n\geq m$.
An ordered collection of numbers ending at a final index.
An ordered collection indexed by integers $n\geq m$.
An ordered collection whose elements must be real numbers.

questions.question: What feature distinguishes sequences from sets in the interpretation?
Which notation denotes an infinite sequence?
Which listed sequence oscillates?
How is a sequence described as a function?
options: Sequences are functions defined on intervals of real numbers.
Sequences are functions defined on subsets of the integers.
Sequences are functions whose values must be integers.
Sequences are functions defined on finite sets of integers only.

questions.question: Which statement about the elements of a sequence is supported by the definition?
options: They must all be distinct from one another.
They must form a convergent list of numbers.
They must be ordered by size, from small to large.
They may be numbers, vectors, or functions.

questions.question: If a sequence starts at $m = 0$, which term appears first in the displayed form?
Which pair represents the same terms but a different order?
Why is the starting integer $m$ part of the notation $(a_n)_{n\geq m}$?
options: It sets the value of the first term equal to $m$.
It gives the number of terms in the sequence.
It specifies where the ordered terms begin.
It is the index from which the sequence converges.

questions.question: Which statement best links sequences to limiting behaviour?
options: Limits depend only on the set of values, not their order.
Only the first few terms decide whether a sequence converges.
Order lets us study term behaviour as the index advances.
A sequence has a limit exactly when its terms are ordered by size.

questions.question: Which object is better described as a set rather than a sequence?
Suppose $(a_n)_{n\geq 1}$ and $(b_n)_{n\geq 1}$ contain the same values but in a different order. Which conclusion is safest?
options: They must be the same sequence, because only membership matters.
They are undefined unless all terms are rational.
They need not be the same sequence, because order matters.

questions.question: In the notation $(a_n)_{n\ge m}$, what does the index $n$ do?
options: It equals the value of each term, so that $a_n = n$.
It labels each term's position in the order.
It must run over all integers, including negative ones.
It is a fixed number chosen once for the whole sequence.

questions.question: If $a_1=1$ and $a_{n+1}=a_n+2$, what is $a_4$?
How many distinct values appear in the range of the sequence $1,1,1,\ldots$?
For the sequence $a_n=n^2$ with $n\ge1$, what is $a_3$?
For $a_n=(-1)^n$ with $n\ge1$, what are the first three terms?
Which object is a finite sequence?
What does it mean to view a sequence as a function?
options: Each term is assigned exactly one integer index.
Each integer index is assigned exactly one term.
Each real number $x$ is assigned exactly one term.
Each integer index may be assigned several terms.
